flawed_step: The claim that choosing the shortest remaining interval is always safe: a short interval can overlap two longer intervals that don't overlap each other.
counterexample: Intervals A=[0,10) (duration 10), B=[9,12) (duration 3), C=[11,22) (duration 11); all durations distinct. The greedy picks the unique shortest interval B. B overlaps A (on [9,10)) and C (on [11,12)), so both are discarded and the greedy returns {B}, size 1. A and C don't overlap (10 <= 11), so {A,C} is a valid schedule of size 2. 1 < 2.
assessment_summary: Shortest-duration-first greedy is not optimal for interval scheduling. With A=[0,10), B=[9,12), C=[11,22), the greedy returns only {B}, while the optimum {A,C} has size 2. The durations are distinct, so the greedy is strictly worse under every tie-breaking rule.
